read.sections.0.heading.back: Small actions can help a community
read.sections.0.heading.source: Small actions can help a community

read.sections.0.text.back: Contributing means giving your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to be a big campaign, because everyday actions are important too. A student can read together with younger children, translate for people who are new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work in a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child states that children have the right to give their views on matters that affect them. The Convention also states that children are free to set up or join groups and meet together.
read.sections.0.text.source: To contribute means to give your time, skills or help to make something better. Contributing does not have to mean a big campaign, because everyday actions matter too. A learner can read with a younger child, translate for someone who is new, keep a shared room clean or join a club. These actions help people learn, feel welcome and share the work of a community. The United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child says that children have the right to give their views on things that affect them. It also says children are free to start or join groups and to meet together.

The list says children can give their views. It also says they can join groups.

read.sections.1.heading.back: Start with evidence and work together
read.sections.1.heading.source: Start with evidence and work together

read.sections.1.text.back: Students at Hillside Learning Centre noticed rubbish near the bus stop outside the centre. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry online post, might hurt people's feelings and will not solve the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. Together with a teacher, the students ask the people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include the bus users, the students themselves and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns that evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager, with one clear suggestion, such as a new rubbish bin. Working together with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.
read.sections.1.text.source: Learners at Hillside Learning Centre noticed litter near the bus stop outside. They had three ideas. Idea 1, an angry post online, might upset people and would not fix the problem. Idea 2 starts with evidence. With a teacher, the learners ask people who use the bus stop what is missing. People who are affected by a problem are called stakeholders. Here, the stakeholders include bus users, the learners and the centre manager. Idea 3 turns the evidence into a short, polite letter to the manager with one clear suggestion, such as a new bin. Working with others makes a plan fairer and more likely to succeed.

read.sections.2.text.note: Translator: 'Clean-up' is translated as 'gotong-royong' throughout (also in the evidence card, checks, write example and picture title). It is the natural Malaysian word for a community clean-up, but it suggests community-wide work. Check that it fits a small learner activity, or use 'aktiviti pembersihan' instead. Back-translation check: The translator's 'gotong-royong' flag still stands (see evidence.cards.0.cases.1.body). Also check 'imbas kembali'.
read.sections.2.text.back: A good contribution is safe. Before the clean-up, the students talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take photos of the rubbish, the photos must not show anyone's face or personal information. You do not need to speak in front of a crowd, make an online post or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was involved? What will we do differently next time? Even small changes, such as a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.
read.sections.2.text.source: Good contributions are safe. Before a clean-up, the learners talk to a teacher and get permission from the centre manager. They plan to use gloves and bags, and they arrange for the rubbish to be taken away. If they take a photo of the litter, it should not show anyone's face or private information. You never need to speak in public, post online or take risks to contribute. After acting, look back and ask: What changed? Who was included? What would we do differently next time? Even a small change, like a cleaner bus stop, can make a difference.

read.sections.2.simpler.back: Helping must be safe. First, the students talk with a teacher. The centre manager gives permission. They use gloves and bags. They plan where the rubbish will be taken. write.example.back: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will investigate what is missing. Together with our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask for permission from our teacher and the centre manager to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish into bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. After that, we will check the bus stop once more and ask users whether they see a change.
write.example.source: Our goal is to make the bus stop outside our centre cleaner. First, we will find out what is missing. With our teacher, we will ask five bus users. We will ask our teacher and the centre manager for permission to hold a one-hour clean-up. To stay safe, we will wear gloves, work in pairs and put the rubbish in bags for the centre to take away. We will not take photos of people. Afterwards, we will check the bus stop again and ask users if they see a change.

watch.summary.back: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to the voices of young people and to act. This video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and real chances to change what happens. You do not need to talk to world leaders to bring about change. You can also help in small and safe ways, such as reading together with younger children or keeping a shared space clean.
watch.summary.source: In this UNICEF video, young people share messages for world leaders. They talk about how climate change affects their lives and the places where they live. They ask leaders to listen to young people and to act. The video shows that young people have good ideas about problems that affect them. But ideas need to reach the right people. For this to work, young people need facts, help from adults and a real chance to change what happens. You do not have to speak to world leaders to make a difference. You can also help in small, safe ways, like reading with a younger child or keeping a shared space clean.
